headline: Alberta votes to stay part of Canada

sources.title: Alberta voters reject separation from Canada, early results show (Al Jazeera)
Alberta rejects move toward independence from Canada in a victory for Carney (NBC News / AP)
Alberta votes overwhelmingly to remain part of Canada, projections suggest (BBC News)

chunks.text: On Monday, October 19, 2026, people in the Canadian province of Alberta voted in a [[referendum]]. They were asked whether to stay in Canada or start a [[legal process]] that could lead to a second vote on {{breaking away}}. Early results on October 20 showed about three in four voters chose to stay. About one in four [[backed]] the path toward separation. Delays at about 100 [[polling stations]] {{held up}} the results by more than two hours.

verbs.correct: To leave a country and form a new one
verbs.wrong: To hold a vote on the same question
verbs.why: Some regions want to break away from their country. Some islands want to break away and become their own country. Voters were asked about a second vote on breaking away from Canada.

verbs.wrong: To count something a second time
verbs.why: Heavy snow often holds up the trains. A long line at the bank holds me up every Friday. Delays at about 100 polling stations held up the results by more than two hours.

chunks.text: Alberta is rich in oil. Many separatists there are angry with Canada's [[federal government]] in Ottawa. They say its [[environmental policies]] have hurt the province's [[oil industry]]. A citizens' group collected about 300,000 [[signatures]] asking for a vote on separation. A judge {{threw out}} that [[petition]], saying it had failed to [[consult]] Indigenous First Nations. Alberta's [[premier]], who opposes separation, {{went ahead with}} a [[nonbinding]] vote anyway.

verbs.correct: To refuse to accept a request
verbs.wrong: To sign a request for a new law
verbs.why: A judge sometimes throws out a weak case. The city council often throws out plans for new towers. A judge threw out the petition because it had failed to consult Indigenous First Nations.

verbs.correct: To still do something that was planned
verbs.wrong: To ask a court to change a decision
verbs.why: The school goes ahead with the trip, even in the rain. Many couples go ahead with their wedding plans after a small problem. Alberta's premier went ahead with a nonbinding vote after a judge threw out the petition.

chunks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney, who {{grew up}} in Alberta, said Albertans had made "a clear choice." The premier said the result showed [[widespread]] support for staying in Canada. Before the vote, Carney and other national leaders {{spoke out}} against separation. Elon Musk, a well-known supporter of U.S. President Donald Trump, wrote online that Alberta should separate. The Associated Press reported that Trump's [[trade war]] and [[threats]] to make Canada a U.S. state helped Carney {{win over}} voters in Alberta.

verbs.wrong: To work somewhere for many years
verbs.why: Many people grow up in small towns. Most kids in my town grow up near the ocean. Prime Minister Mark Carney grew up in Alberta.

verbs.correct: To say publicly what you think
verbs.wrong: To visit many towns to meet voters
verbs.why: Many doctors speak out against smoking. She speaks out when a rule is unfair. Before the vote, Carney and other national leaders spoke out against separation.
A kind teacher wins over a shy class. A new coach often wins over the fans with a strong first season. Trump's trade war and threats helped Carney win over voters in Alberta.

chunks.text: [[Separatist]] leaders say they will not {{back down}}. One leader called the vote a [[first step]] and said the movement would {{carry on}}. He had hoped for 30 percent of the vote. The early results {{fell short of}} that number. At one separatist event in Edmonton, people {{packed up}} and went home. Some separatists now want to {{push the premier out}} as leader of her party. [[Official results]] could take days to {{come in}}.

verbs.correct: To accept defeat and stop trying
verbs.wrong: To hold a rally for supporters
verbs.why: My brother never backs down in an argument. The workers don't back down until they get a fair deal. Separatist leaders say they will not back down after the vote.
The band carries on after the singer leaves. We carry on with the game in light rain. One separatist leader said the movement would carry on.

verbs.correct: To not reach a goal or number
verbs.wrong: To change a goal to a new number
verbs.why: Many students fall short of their reading goals. The money often falls short of what the school needs. The early results fell short of the 30 percent one separatist leader hoped for.

verbs.correct: To gather your things and leave
verbs.wrong: To cheer loudly for a long time
verbs.why: The workers pack up their tools at five o'clock. After a game, many fans pack up and go home. At one separatist event in Edmonton, people packed up and went home.

verbs.correct: To force someone to leave a job
verbs.why: Some companies push older workers out. Angry members sometimes push a leader out of the club. Some separatists now want to push the premier out as leader of her party.

verbs.wrong: To be checked by a judge
verbs.why: Election results come in late at night. Test scores come in at the end of June. Official results in Alberta could take days to come in.

mainIdea.s: Early counts show that about three in four Alberta voters want to remain in Canada. Separatist leaders lost, but they say their push to leave the country will carry on.
mainIdea.why: About three in four voters chose to stay in Canada. Separatist leaders say they will not back down, and one said the movement would carry on.

mainIdea.s: Most Albertans rejected a plan that could have led to separation from Canada. Because of this clear result, the separatist groups now say they will end their campaign.
mainIdea.why: Close, but separatist leaders say they will not back down. Some of them even want to push the premier out as leader of her party.

mainIdea.s: Quebec's newly elected provincial government has promised to hold a vote on independence by 2030. Its leaders say the province needs more control over its own affairs.
mainIdea.why: This story is about Alberta. Early results show most voters chose to stay in Canada, while one in four backed the path toward breaking away.

tf.s: Most Alberta voters chose to stay part of Canada.
tf.why: About three in four voters chose to stay. About one in four backed the path toward breaking away.

tf.s: Alberta's premier wants the province to break away from Canada.
tf.why: The premier opposes separation. She still went ahead with a nonbinding vote.

tf.s: Separatist leaders say they will not back down after the vote.
tf.why: One leader called the vote a first step and said the movement would carry on.

tf.s: The two sides finished nearly even in the early results.
tf.why: About three in four voters chose to stay. The separation side fell short of even the 30 percent one leader hoped for.

tf.s: Carney and other national leaders spoke out against separation.
tf.why: Before the vote, they told voters that Alberta should stay in Canada.

tf.s: Some separatists want to push the premier out as party leader.
tf.why: They want a new leader for her party, one who supports their cause.

lines.text: Did you see the results from Alberta?
Only the headline. Did they vote to {{break away}} from Canada?
No. About three in four people voted to stay. The stay side won [[by a mile]].
Wait, was it really a vote on independence?
Not quite. It was a vote on starting a process toward a second vote.
Why did the premier hold it if she wants Alberta to stay in Canada?
A big petition asked for one. A judge {{threw it out}}, but she {{went ahead with}} a nonbinding vote.
He {{grew up}} in Alberta, so this vote is [[close to his heart]]. He called it a clear choice.
I heard the trade war helped him {{win over}} a lot of voters there.
That's what the Associated Press reported. He and other leaders {{spoke out}} against separation, too.
So is the separatist movement finished?
Its leaders say they won't {{back down}}. One said the movement will {{carry on}}.
Maybe, but one leader hoped for 30 percent, and they {{fell short of}} that.
When will we know the final numbers?
Official results could take days to {{come in}}. Some separatists also want to {{push the premier out}}.
So we'll know more [[once the dust settles]]. It sounds like the separatists are in this [[for the long haul]].

expressions.def: Used to say that someone won or was better by a very large amount
ex: Our team won the game by a mile.
Her cake was the best one by a mile.

expressions.def: Used to say that something matters to a person in a deep, personal way
ex: The children's hospital is close to his heart.

expressions.def: Used to say that people are serious and plan to do what they say
ex: The new coach means business, so practice starts at six.

expressions.def: Used to talk about the time when things become calm and clear again
ex: We can talk about the new budget once the dust settles.
Once the dust settles, the team will choose a new captain.

expressions.def: Used to say that something will last or continue for a long time
ex: We bought this house for the long haul.
She joined the company for the long haul.
